title: Review: Plant transport: phloem and translocation; Chromosomes, karyotypes and genome organisation; Genes, the genetic code and genomes; Transcription
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GE04a#t4 term and clue written for the game; GE04a#t1 term and clue written for the game; EX11#t4 term and clue written for the game; GE04a#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD05a#N.4b, EX11#N.5, GE03#N.9a, GE04a#N.11, CD05a#N.8, EX11#N.8, GE03#N.5a, GE04a#N.10, EX11#N.12a, GE03#N.3a, GE04a#N.3a, GE04a#N.5. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Phosphodiester bond
items.clue: Link formed between adjacent nucleotides, building the backbone of the new mRNA.

items.label: Transcription
items.clue: Making an RNA copy of a gene from one DNA strand; the first stage of gene expression.

items.label: Sink
items.clue: Place where sugars leave the phloem to be used or stored, such as a root, meristem or fruit.

items.label: RNA polymerase
items.clue: Enzyme that binds at the start of a gene and joins adjacent nucleotides of the new transcript.

questions.stem: A line of eukaryotic cells grown in a laboratory carries a mutation that greatly reduces the amount of histone protein the cells make. Which prediction about the DNA in the nuclei of these cells is best supported?

options.text: Its DNA will be less tightly packed, so its chromosomes will be less condensed.
Its DNA will have a changed base sequence, as histones set the order of its bases.
Its two DNA strands will come apart, as histones hold the base pairs together.
Its chromosomes will lose some genes, as histones are sections of the DNA.

questions.explanation: Histones are the proteins that DNA winds around to become condensed. With far fewer histones, less DNA can be wound and packed, so the chromosomes are expected to be less condensed.

questions.stem: Which feature of a sieve tube element helps sap to flow along the phloem?

options.text: It is dead and empty like a xylem vessel, so there is nothing inside the cell to slow the flow of sap.
Its end walls are solid plates that hold the sap under pressure so that it flows faster along the tube.
It contains many mitochondria, whose ATP is used to push the sap along the tube towards the sink.
It has lost its nucleus and most of its cytoplasm and organelles, so little inside it obstructs the sap.

questions.stem: The gene for human insulin has been inserted into bacteria, which then translate it into a polypeptide with the same amino acid sequence as the polypeptide made in human cells. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?

options.text: Universality: bacteria and humans have the same genes, so the bacterium already had an insulin gene.
Degeneracy: each codon can be read as several amino acids, so the bacterium can make any protein.
Complementary pairing: bacterial tRNA anticodons pair directly with the bases of the inserted DNA.
Universality: the bacterium's tRNAs assign exactly the same amino acids to the codons as human cells do.

questions.stem: α-Amanitin, a toxin from the death cap mushroom, blocks the RNA polymerase that makes mRNA in eukaryotic cells. It has no effect on DNA polymerase or on ribosomes. Which prediction about liver cells exposed to it is correct?

options.text: DNA replication stops, because the cells can no longer separate their DNA strands.
Translation of mRNA already in the cytoplasm stops at once.
No new mRNA is made, so protein synthesis falls as the existing mRNA is broken down.
The DNA of the cells' genes is damaged, so their base sequences change.

questions.explanation: Without RNA polymerase there is no transcription and no new mRNA. Proteins are made only until the existing mRNA runs out.

questions.stem: Each chromatid of human chromosome 1 contains one DNA molecule about 85 mm long. When the cell divides, the condensed chromosome is about 10 µm long (illustrative round value). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The DNA is about 8.5 times longer than the chromosome, because it is wound round histones and coiled further.
The DNA is about 8 500 times longer than the chromosome, because it is wound round histones and coiled further.
The DNA is about 8 500 times longer than the chromosome, because packing removes bases to shorten the molecule.
The DNA is about 8 500 times longer than the chromosome, because the double helix twists tighter with no proteins involved.

questions.stem: In spring, sugars stored in the roots of a deciduous tree are converted to sucrose and carried in the phloem to the opening buds. Which statement about this transport is correct?

options.text: Mitochondria in the companion cells provide the ATP that physically drives the sap along the sieve tubes up to the buds.
Companion cells in the root use ATP to load sucrose into the sieve tubes, and the sap flows up to the buds, the sinks.
Sap cannot move upwards in the phloem, so the sugars must instead be carried up to the buds in the xylem.
The sieve tube elements must first be killed and emptied, as in xylem, before any sap is able to flow through them.

questions.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?

options.text: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.
Some amino acids are coded for by two bases and some by three bases.

questions.explanation: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids; for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the radioactive uridine data?

options.text: RNA is made in the cytoplasm and then moves into the nucleus.
RNA is made and translated in the nucleus, then broken down in the cytoplasm.
RNA is made in the nucleus and then moves to the cytoplasm.
DNA moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, carrying the radioactive label.

questions.explanation: The label appears first in the nucleus, then shifts to the cytoplasm when almost no new labelled RNA is being made. It must have moved out.

questions.stem: A young leaf near a shoot tip is still expanding. It imports sucrose through the phloem. Weeks later, fully grown, the same leaf exports sucrose. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Now it makes more sugar than it uses, so its companion cells load sucrose: it has become a source.
When young, the leaf received its sugar in the xylem, because phloem only ever carries sap out of leaves.
As the leaf aged, its sieve tubes died and became lignified, which reversed the direction of flow.
Mitochondria in the leaf's companion cells switched from pushing sap in to pushing sap out.

questions.stem: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?

options.text: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.

questions.explanation: 4 × 4 = 16 is fewer than 20; 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 is more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

questions.stem: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?

options.text: UACGCAU
AUGCGUA
UAGCGAU
ATGCGTA

questions.explanation: Each RNA base is complementary to the template base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, giving AUGCGUA.

questions.stem: During transcription, what holds each RNA nucleotide in position against the DNA template strand while it is being added to the growing RNA?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break again when the RNA is released.
Covalent bonds made by RNA polymerase between the RNA base and the DNA base opposite it.
Hydrogen bonds between identical bases, so the RNA is an exact copy of the template.
Hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine, since RNA contains the same four bases as DNA.
